<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is VvvebJs – an open-source, drag & drop page builder JavaScript library built with vanilla JavaScript and Bootstrap 5 (with no external dependencies). It provides a fully interactive page editor where users can assemble pages by dragging and dropping components and blocks, with supporting features like file management, undo/redo, live editing (using CodeMirror), and optional server-side support for saving pages (via PHP or Node).

Below are detailed instructions and guidelines for drawing an accurate and detailed system design diagram for VvvebJs:

1. Project Type and Purpose
   - This is a JavaScript-based page builder library primarily focused on the front end.
   - Its purpose is to allow non-technical users to design and modify web pages interactively.
   - It is extensible and supports additional components, plugins, and even file management with optional backend support.

2. Analyze the File Structure
   - There are several top-level directories and files that indicate the architectural components:
     • The root contains configuration files (Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml, package.json, gulpfile.js) for development and deployment.
     • The demos in the “demo” folder give examples of pages (e.g., album, blog, carousel, landing) that the editor can work with.
     • The “libs” directory is crucial; it contains subdirectories for:
         – AOS (animation library)
         – Codemirror (for live code editing)
         – Builder components and plugins (e.g., builder.js, components-bootstrap5.js, various plugin files)
         – Media and other helper libraries.
     • Style assets reside in “css” and “scss” directories (plus fonts and images) and indicate the use of Bootstrap along with custom CSS/SCSS.
     • PHP files (e.g., editor.php, save.php, upload.php) and Node.js script (save.js) indicate optional backend endpoints.
   - The project also contains an extensive nested “resources” folder holding SVG icon sets, showing that icons are an integral part of the UI.

3. Key Components to Include in the Diagram
   a. Editor / UI Layer
      - Editor Interface: Represented by “editor.html” and “editor.php”. This is the main entry point where users interact with the page builder.
      - UI Components: The drag-and-drop interface, live code editor (with CodeMirror), undo/redo, and visual panels.
   
   b. Builder Core / JavaScript Library
      - Core Builder Engine: Indicated by “libs/builder/builder.js”, which orchestrates the page building, component insertion, and user interactions.
      - Component Modules: Various components found in “libs/builder/components-*.js” (for Bootstrap 5, widgets, server components, etc.) that define available blocks, sections, and other elements.
      - Plugin System: Plugins (e.g., plugin-ai-assistant.js, plugin-ckeditor.js, plugin-google-fonts.js, etc.) allow the system to be extended. Mark these as optional modules integrated into the core.
      - Inputs and Undo Manager: Outline the “libs/builder/inputs.js” and “libs/builder/undo.js” (handling events and providing undo/redo functionality).
   
   c. File and Page Management
      - File Manager: Represented by “Vvveb.FileManager” functionalities (see in the example snippet) to manage and load pages.
      - Save/Upload Handlers: Include “save.php”, “upload.php”, and “save.js” that allow saving/exporting pages.
   
   d. External Libraries and Dependencies
      - Integration with Bootstrap 5 and possibly CodeMirror for code editing.
      - Other helper libraries such as Codemirror, Swiper, AOS (Animate on Scroll) that contribute to the user experience.
      - The extensive icons collection in the “resources/svg/icons” directory should be represented as an asset repository consumed by the UI.
   
   e. Build and Deployment Utilities
      - The build process is managed by Gulp (gulpfile.js) and has tasks for compiling SCSS, generating HTML from templates (especially in demo/landing), and creating screenshots.
      - Docker and Docker Compose configuration for local development and deployment.

4. Relationships and Data Flow
   - Draw directional arrows from the Editor UI (front end) to the Builder Core, showing how user actions trigger JavaScript functions.
   - Connect the Builder Core to component modules and plugins to show how the system dynamically loads behavior for each component.
   - Illustrate the two modes of saving: one arrow for PHP-based saving via “save.php” (in a traditional server setup) and one for Node-based operations (save.js), highlighting the optional backend.
   - Include the File Manager component and its interaction with the Builder Core (loading pages, managing assets).
   - Mark the build process as a separate, development-time utility that compiles SCSS into CSS and bundles assets.

5. Visualizing Patterns and Technologies
   - Distinguish between the core library, plugins, and external dependencies. For example, you might use rectangles for core modules, circles for plugins, and icons or different colors for external libraries.
   - If applicable, show an MVC/MVVM-style layering where:
     • The “View” layer is the Editor UI (editor.html/php)
     • The “Controller/Service” layer is the Builder Core managing interactions
     • The “Model” layer is represented by saved templates or state management (managed via FileManager, undo manager, and backend saving features).
   - Emphasize modularity and extensibility as key design principles, illustrating that new components or plugins can plug into the core without breaking the architecture.

6. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram
   - Because this is a front-end page builder but with optional back-end support:
     • Clearly separate the client-side (Editor UI, Builder Core, Drag and Drop components, live code editing, plugin integration) from server-side functionalities (PHP, Node scripts for saving and image uploads).
     • Include the development/build tools (Gulp, Docker) as a separate “build & deployment” block to avoid muddling the runtime architecture.
     • Use directional arrows to indicate interactions (for example, user actions on the Editor UI cause events in the Builder Core) and response flows (e.g., saving a page).
   - Include labels for every component:
     • “Editor Interface (HTML/PHP)”
     • “Builder Core (builder.js and associated modules)”
     • “Component Library (components-bootstrap5.js, components-widgets.js, etc.)”
     • “Plugins (plugin-*)”
     • “File Manager”
     • “Live Code Editor (CodeMirror integration)”
     • “Backend Save/Upload Handler (save.php, save.js)”
     • “Development Tools (Gulp, Docker, etc.)”
   - Use clear color coding or shapes (e.g., rounded rectangles for client-side modules, cylinders for storage/asset management, hexagons for plugins, etc.) to distinguish layers and types of components.

7. Final Diagram Best Practices
   - Ensure every component is clearly labeled.
   - Use arrows to indicate the flow of data and control (for example, from UI actions to JavaScript engine functions and then to the File Manager).
   - Incorporate a legend to explain color coding or shapes used in the diagram.
   - Divide the diagram into logical sections (UI, Core Library, Plugins, Backend Integration, and Build/Deployment Tools) to make it easier to understand.
   - Don’t shy away from adding extra granularity – separating components as much as possible to capture all essential architectural elements.

Using these guidelines, you should produce a system design diagram that not only represents the architecture clearly but also serves as a useful reference for both understanding and extending VvvebJs. This approach emphasizes modularity, separation of concerns, and integration between the various parts of the system while being tailored to its specific usage as a drag-and-drop page builder library.
</explanation>
